Could you break down the relationship between different types of magnetism from the perspective of spinning electrons and chemical bonds; dia,. Ferro, para.. etc

Material magnetism is an extremely complicated topic, and I cannot really do it justice in a short comment like this. But really short: you get a coupling between electron spin (intrinsic dipolar magnetic moment of electrons) and the orbit around the nucleus (charge going around in circles gives another dipolar magnetic moment). But those orbitals depend on the kind of crystal structure you have, which depends on the specific nature of the chemical bonds etc. So all these interactions influence each other, until you eventual end up with these possibilities:

  1. Non-magnetic. No atomic magnetic moment persists.
  2. Ferromagnetic. Neighboring magnetic moments try to align.
  3. Ferrimagnetic. Two different magnetic moments which act ferromagnetically amongst each other.
  4. Antiferromagnetic. Neighboring magnetic moments try to align counter to their neighbors. This can lead to frustrated magnetic materials and spin waves.
  5. Paramagnetic. Typically when ferromagnets/antiferromagnets are heated above their Curie/Néel temperature. Atomic magnetic moments are not zero, but all moments are oriented randomly, giving a total net magnetic moment of (almost) zero.
  6. Diamagnetic. The material will try to (partially) cancel an externally applied magnetic field. Most striking in superconductors, which will perfectly cancel all magnetic fields, called the Meissner effect.
